issues.legal_issue: A civil suit based on title and possession is not barred merely because a revenue officer previously ordered ejectment in a proceeding concerning an alleged landlord-tenant relationship.
material_facts: The appellant sought ejectment of the respondents in a revenue proceeding, claiming that they were his shikmi tenants, and the revenue officer found that the appellant was the khatedar.
The respondents brought a civil suit asserting their own title to the land and seeking possession.
issues.conclusion: The revenue proceeding did not bar the civil court from hearing the respondents’ suit based on title and possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil courts may hear civil suits unless their jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred; a party asserting exclusion must establish it, and an ouster is strictly construed. Section 200(1) of the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, read with section 71, did not exclude jurisdiction because section 71 presupposed a landlord-tenant relationship and did not empower the revenue officer to decide title. The court distinguished Gokhul Sahu v. Jodu Nundun Roy and Jatindra Nath Chowdhury v. Azizur Rahaman Shanao because the provisions considered there were not in pari materia.

predicates.civil_title_and_possession_suit: A claimant brought a civil suit asserting title to land and seeking possession.
predicates.prior_revenue_ejectment_proceeding: An opposing claimant previously sought ejectment of the claimant in a revenue proceeding on the basis of an alleged landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.revenue_proceeding_did_not_determine_tit: The revenue proceeding concerned ejectment based on the alleged landlord-tenant relationship and did not decide ownership of the land.

issues.definition: When a civil claimant seeks title and possession after a revenue ejectment proceeding that did not determine title, the civil court may hear the title suit.

issues.legal_issue: An entry in a land-rights register is rebuttable evidence in a civil suit based on title and does not itself bar that suit.
material_facts: The register of rights recorded the appellant as the holder of the disputed land.
The respondents relied on oral and documentary evidence to establish their title, and the courts found that evidence sufficient to rebut the register entry’s presumption of correctness.
issues.conclusion: The register entry was only presumptive evidence, its presumption was rebutted by the respondents’ evidence, and it did not prevent the civil suit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 89(2), 93(1)–(2), and 95 of the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act provide for entries concerning landholders, summary decisions about disputed entries, and a presumption that register entries are correct until the contrary is proved. The ability to rebut an entry in a civil title suit is consistent with section 93(2), and section 200(1) does not impliedly bar such a suit.

predicates.civil_title_suit: A claimant brought a civil suit to establish title to land.
predicates.land_register_entry_supports_opposing_cl: The land-rights register recorded the opposing claimant as the holder of the land.
predicates.contrary_evidence_establishes_claimant_t: The claimant presented oral or documentary evidence that the court found established the claimant’s title despite the register entry.

issues.definition: In a civil title suit, an entry supporting the opposing claimant is rebutted when the claimant presents evidence that the court finds establishes the claimant’s title.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings on title and the rebuttal of a land-register entry are not open to challenge in an appeal by special leave merely by rearguing the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that the respondents had title and that their evidence rebutted the presumption arising from the register entry.
The High Court reached the same conclusion and considered the evidence, including additional notifications.
The appellant sought to contest the concurrent factual findings in an appeal by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not permit the appellant to challenge the correctness of the concurrent factual findings in the appeal by special leave.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court was not justified in allowing the appellant to canvass the correctness of concurrent findings of fact in these circumstances. The Court noted that the High Court should have accepted the first appellate court’s finding rather than review the evidence again.

predicates.appeal_by_special_leave: A party brought an appeal by special leave from a lower court judgment.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings_on_title: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual findings about title.
predicates.challenge_requires_reweighing_evidence: The appellant sought to overturn those findings by asking the reviewing court to reassess the evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal by special leave, concurrent factual findings on title are not reopened when overturning them would require reassessing the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for possession brought within the applicable limitation period after dispossession is not time-barred merely because it began as a suit for declaration of title and was later amended to seek possession.
material_facts: The respondents initially sued for a declaration of title and were dispossessed after filing the suit.
They later amended the plaint to seek possession, and the suit was brought within twelve years of their dispossession.
issues.conclusion: The suit for possession was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Because the suit was outside the scope of the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, limitation was governed by the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. Article 142 applied to the suit for possession, and the suit was within time because it was filed within twelve years of dispossession.

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession_after_disposse: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession after being dispossessed of land.
predicates.suit_within_applicable_limitation_period: The claimant brought the suit within the limitation period applicable to the possession claim.

issues.definition: A civil possession suit brought within its applicable limitation period after dispossession is not time-barred.
